data.title: Live updates: Trump campaigns in South Carolina, Vance heads to Ohio
data.description:
President Trump is set to hit the campaign trail on Friday in an attempt to give Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) one last boost before the special GOP primary runoff on Tuesday.

Graham, a political newcomer who replaced her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), is going up against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) for the opportunity to snag the Republican seat in the Palmetto State.

Darline Graham’s inexperience showed on the debate stage on Tuesday when she was unable to answer a national security question, raising uncertainty about her ability to serve in the Senate.

Vice President Vance travels on Friday to his Ohio hometown, Middletown, for an economic speech. On Thursday night, he tried to offer reassurance that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s plan to shrink the nation’s debt and shore up the bond market is on track.

“So, even though the debt is too high, even though we inherited this debt bomb from the Biden administration, we actually do have a plan to get the economy growing faster than the debt and that’s the most important thing,” the vice president said.

The Supreme Court could weigh in Friday on an appeals court ruling that aims to halt construction of the White House ballroom.

The president is also pushing his relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, repeatedly calling for a meeting with the leader and reducing joint military exercises with South Korea. Experts are warning ties to North Korea and reductions in joint military exercises with its neighbors may jeopardize the American relationship with South Korea.

IndyCar will take over the District of Columbia this weekend, with the Freedom 250 race on Saturday and Sunday. It may cause a “little bit of carnage,” the IndyCar chief said.

Follow live below.

data.title: What's with Trump's war against the US Navy?
data.description:
August is traditionally silly season for news stories, and President Trump does not disappoint. So far, he has insisted that the Navy go back to using steam, decreed that the Strait of Hormuz will be a U.S. territory, and demanded that new aircraft carriers be redesigned to make them look “better.”

The Hormuz thing is just weird. For one thing, for a country to own a territory, it must permanently physically occupy and control it. You can’t occupy a body of water, and certainly not permanently. Trump’s blockade — which doesn’t actually control the strait — is no help. Eventually, the Fifth Fleet, like the USS Abraham Lincoln, is going to have to sail away, whereas Iran is physically right there and not going anywhere. 

More fundamentally, you cannot win a conflict by simply declaring victory. Trump started the Iran war without thinking through the consequences and has painted himself into a corner. That he is “claiming” the Strait of Hormuz rather than wrestling with the very serious problems we now face is a real concern. Perhaps he will next order the U.S. Navy to gather seashells, a la Caligula. 

Trump’s fixation on steam catapults for aircraft carriers goes back to his first term. He has now decreed that the new electromagnetic catapults already in use are “no good” and that new carriers should go back to steam. It is not entirely clear where all this is coming from, but it is possible that Trump’s analysis is based on the opening scene of “Top Gun.”  

It certainly isn’t based on any sort of expertise. In the words of Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), I’ve launched off the front of aircraft carriers hundreds of times, have a Master’s degree in aeronautical engineering, and am a test pilot and even I wouldn’t suggest to the Navy how to engineer specific systems on its ships.” Trump, in contrast, appears to think magnets stop working if they get wet.

If there were a prize for this sort of thing, it would probably go to Trump’s foray into naval architecture. New aircraft carriers have a tower in the back of the ship rather than in the middle like they did in World War 2. The new design allows more planes to take off and land in an hour, making the carrier that much more deadly and effective. But Trump thinks the new design doesn’t look nice, so he is ordering that the tower be moved so that the new carriers look more like they did 80 years ago.

As weird as all this is, none of it is the slightest bit amusing. It is simply further evidence that Trump may be struggling with dementia and that his ability to make rational decisions is decaying by the day.

Worse, these bad decisions are having real consequences, on real people. His efforts to unilaterally redesign American warships just to suit his aesthetic preferences will not only cause delays and cost billions of dollars, it will make those ships less effective when they finally are built. Truly, it’s unforgivable is that the men and women in the U.S. Navy are now suffering because of the foolishness of their commander in chief. 

The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for nine months and at sea for more than 200 days, the longest stretch at sea in modern history. The long and unplanned deployment — a direct result of Trump’s poorly conceived war with Iran — has left the ship in terrible condition. There were already food shortages back in April and conditions have only gotten worse. Trump’s response is to call these reports “fake news” and claim that the USS Abraham Lincoln had not really been at sea all that long. 

Love him or hate him, you can just imagine what the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) — a real-life war hero — would have had to say about all this. Sadly, backbone and defiance have long been bred out of the current crop of congressional Republicans, so their thunderous silence comes as no surprise. Not only are they not holding the Trump administration to account, some of them are actively defending it. Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas), for example, said he didn’t “make much” of the reports about conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Feeding sailors and designing aircraft carriers are not partisan issues. In fact, they are not issues at all — just things that must be properly done. Taking a stand on these things is not asking for much, but apparently it is too much to ask of Republicans. We may have come to expect this kind of cowardice, but we should not accept it.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney who served as Southern California chair for John McCain’s primary campaign in 2008.

data.title: Iran labels new US sanctions 'unjust'
data.description:
Mohammed Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament, pushed back Friday against “unjust” U.S. economic sanctions placed on the country by the Trump administration earlier this week. 

“We must plan for the unjust sanctions so that we can overcome them,” Qalibaf told a group of economic representatives in Baghdad, according to a message shared on Telegram.

President Trump announced Wednesday that his administration would impose the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Tehran amid negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil-trading waterway in the region. 

“This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” the president wrote on Truth Social. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had previously teased new economic sanctions against Iran, said he would share more details about these measures next week.

“It is a one-two punch. We have ​the [naval] blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” the secretary told ​CNBC on Thursday. “It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this ⁠regime.”  

Iran’s foreign affairs ministry responded Thursday, saying these new sanctions amount to “economic terrorism” in a statement shared by state media. 

“These sanctions, imposed following the wars imposed by U.S.-Israeli regimes against Iran over the past year and a half and their failure to achieve their sinister objectives of forcing the Iranian people to surrender to their illegal and anti-human ambitions, will merely add to the list of crimes committed by the United States against Iran,” the statement said. 

“They will, however, undoubtedly have the slightest effect on the determination of Iranians to safeguard Iran’s independence, dignity and national sovereignty,” the ministry added. 

Major General Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of Iranian Armed Forces, also vowed there will be a “devastating” response to any threat against Iran in a Friday message. 

“With preparedness across land, sea, air, air defence and cyberspace, Iran’s armed forces will respond to the enemy’s new threats with crushing, punishing and devastating responses,” Abdollahi said, according to state media.

data.title: 'Woke' by any other name: Stop erasing the terms of our survival
data.description:
I have watched a word that once helped keep my people alive get turned into a punchline, then a slur, and now, this month, a punchline again, this time by people who are supposed to be on our side.

On Aug. 11, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) sat across from Jonathan Karl on ABC’s “This Week” and, asked about positions held by democratic socialists in 2020, repeated a phrase she attributed to a fellow politician: “Woke 1 was crazy.” She moved on quickly, arguing reasonably that candidates should be judged on where they stand today rather than where they stood five years ago.

Since then, those four words have become part of a larger debate about what Democrats should leave behind from 2020. Some of that reckoning is overdue. But before we turn “woke” into a convenient label for everything that went wrong, we should remember something important: woke was never a branding exercise for Black people. It was an instruction.

I say that as someone who admires Ocasio-Cortez and the power she has built for working people. This isn’t about piling on. It is about asking who gets to declare a chapter of Black political consciousness embarrassing, close the book and move on. Who gets to decide when our vigilance has become inconvenient? Who gets to gatekeep the language of our survival?

“Woke” did not begin as a hashtag or cable news category. Its roots run through generations of Black political consciousness. Marcus Garvey urged Black people to “wake up” to the reality of their condition. In 1938, Lead Belly sang about the Scottsboro Boys, nine Black teenagers falsely accused in Alabama, and warned Black listeners to “stay woke” and keep their eyes open.

That was the point: Stay alert because the danger is real.

In 1962, novelist William Melvin Kelley wrote in The New York Times about white America’s habit of taking Black vernacular, hollowing it out and handing it back as something unrecognizable. Decades later, Erykah Badu helped return “stay woke” to popular consciousness. Then another generation carried it into the streets after Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown and Eric Garner.

After George Floyd’s murder, the phrase went fully mainstream. Then the right seized it.

Florida eventually put the acronym “WOKE” into the title of legislation restricting certain instruction and workplace training involving race. A phrase rooted in Black vigilance became shorthand for nearly anything conservative politicians wanted their voters to fear. Black Americans have seen this before: Language we create to describe our experience gets stripped of context, weaponized and sold back to the country as something dangerous.

What troubles me now is watching parts of the left participate in a softer version of that erasure.

To be clear, there were real excesses in 2020. Some slogans substituted provocation for persuasion. Some activists treated people who shared the goal of a more just society as enemies because they used imperfect language or asked uncomfortable questions. At times, our desire to create safety for marginalized people produced too little room for people to learn, stumble, apologize and grow.

We should be able to say that. A movement incapable of examining its mistakes is not a movement preparing to win.

But society also needs mechanisms for moving people toward justice collectively. Progress requires persuasion as well as protest, grace as well as accountability. Learning those lessons is very different from declaring the awakening itself “crazy.”

That distinction matters because 2020 did not materialize from an internet trend. Millions of people took to the streets after watching a Black man die beneath a police officer’s knee. They were responding to something real. To dismiss that period as an inconvenient pendulum swing is not politically shortsighted. It risks confusing mistakes made in responding to injustice with the injustice that demanded a response.

And the underlying conditions have not disappeared.

I organize voter registration and civic engagement work across Georgia, South Carolina, Mississippi and Texas. Voter rolls are still purged. Polling places still close. Laws still create barriers for people who move, change their names or lack particular forms of identification. Every day, organizers enter communities that politics has ignored and work to make sure their voices are not erased.

That is what staying woke means to me. It isn’t a vocabulary test or a cable news category. It is the discipline of paying attention because history has taught us who pays the price when we don’t.

I’m not interested in defending a word forever. Language changes, movements mature and political strategies should evolve. If “woke” no longer communicates what we need it to communicate, Black communities can be part of the conversation about what comes next.

But there is a difference between retiring a word and rewriting its history. There is a difference between acknowledging that a movement made mistakes and treating the consciousness that animated it as an embarrassment.

America can change the vocabulary. Politics can find a new slogan. What we cannot afford to discard is the vigilance underneath it, because for generations that vigilance has helped Black Americans recognize danger, organize against injustice and claim rights this country too often tried to deny us.

So rename the word if you must — just don’t try to rename our survival.

Andrea D. Pringle is a Democratic campaigner and founder and president of Registration Nation and leads March On PAC, Elect Southern Dems and Future Democrats. She previously held multiple roles at the Democratic National Committee.

data.title: Polls can mislead: Do your own homework before you vote
data.description:
Headlines recently touted a new Siena Research Institute poll claiming that Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York City, enjoys an approval rating of 69 percent.

I don’t believe that. Conversations that I have had with bodega owners, taxi drivers, construction workers and people in many other occupations lead to a different conclusion. New Yorkers cannot stand our smug young socialist mayor.  

Am I not talking to the right people? Do such surveys reliably reflect the mood of the electorate?

After big misses from several polls in recent weeks, people are wondering what to believe. Of course, survey failures are nothing new; President Trump has consistently outperformed his polling, causing many supporters to view the entire industry as suspect. 

For sure, polling can influence voters. If your candidate is crashing in the polls ahead of an election, you may decide it’s not worth voting — that the outcome is preordained and your vote won’t matter. Or, you may decide against donating to a campaign, not wanting to waste your money.

Remember that one month after his 2024 win, then President-elect Trump sued the Des Moines Register and its former pollster, J. Ann Selzer, for “brazen election interference” over a poll published just days before the election.  

Selzer’s Nov. 2 survey showed Democrat Kamala Harris winning reliably red Iowa by 3 to 4 points — a shocking outlier that received a lot of attention at a critical moment in the campaign. Just days later, Trump won Iowa by 13 points. Although Trump later dropped his lawsuit, many agreed that Selzer’s survey had been intended to shake his supporters’ confidence in a race he was quite clearly winning. She quit her job soon thereafter.

Since that 2024 race, the rise of prediction and betting platforms has upped the stakes. People placing bets on political races will have even greater incentives to try to influence or manipulate polling. The smaller the race, the more vulnerable the poll.

Not all polls are trustworthy. Siena is generally deemed accurate, with one group rating it as having a “slight Democratic lean.” But sometimes, even an honest poll can produce a misleading result, as with the Siena poll that had Mamdani fans cheering.  

The institute set out to assess the current state of the governor’s race in New York, and surveyed 811 “likely New York gubernatorial voters.” As such, they included only 227 people in New York City. But that figure is meaningless, as it represents less than .003 percent of the 8.8 million people living in the Big Apple. Of that tiny group, 69 percent approved of the mayor, while only 49 percent gave a thumbs-up to the Democratic Socialists of America, Mamdani’s political home base. That inconsistency typifies the screwy results that come with small samples. If New Yorkers like the mayor, shouldn’t they also like his platform?

Steve Greenberg, who works for the Siena Research Institute, told me that the poll’s samples were starkly different from what Siena might have included if they had aimed to determine Mamdani’s actual popularity.

Because the poll focused on the governor’s race, the survey overweighted areas outside the city. In those regions, the mayor fared poorly, registering approval of only 34 percent in the suburbs and 41 percent upstate. Also, non-white voters were undercounted; some 71 percent of respondents were white, whereas only 10 percent were Black and 13 percent Latino. Also unusual is that of those surveyed, more than half reportedly had incomes above $100,000, whereas the median income in New York State is just shy of $86,000.

Bottom line: because it set out to measure trends in the New York state governor’s race, the Siena poll ended up inadvertently favoring Mamdani, overrepresenting whites with high incomes. The questionable accuracy of the reading, of course, did not preclude Mamdani supporters from jumping on the poll, to tout his supposed popularity.  

Other polls — some big misses — have also recently raised eyebrows. In the run-up to the Democratic primary for an open Senate seat in Michigan, polling showed far-left candidate Abdul El-Sayed running away with the contest, up by double digits over establishment favorite Haley Stevens. On primary night, El-Sayed won by only 1 point. Some theorize that the polling has distorted the popularity of Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates because white liberals are more likely to respond to polls than other Democrats.  

But on the same night, in another Democratic Senate primary, progressive Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) beat out Rep. Angie Craig (D) by nearly 20 percentage points, despite some surveys showing a neck-and-neck contest.

And then there was an actual polling scandal. Median Strategies, a group describing itself as an “independent research and polling” organization on a website that has subsequently disappeared, confessed to creating completely bogus polls. One showed Francesca Hong, a socialist candidate who ran in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor, some 20 or more points ahead of rival Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. Crowley, a moderate, ended up winning. Another poll from Median put incumbent Karen Bass ahead of opponent Nithya Raman in the Los Angeles mayoral contest by almost 12 points.

Median claimed on its now defunct website that it “fabricated the polls as part of a ‘short-term social experiment'” meant to show “how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” as reported by The New York Times. Since Bass posted the poll on X, it spread far and wide, boosting her numbers.

Who was behind that deception and why they did it remain to be seen. But the message is clear: Do not accept polling at face value. Look at the cross-tabs to see who was counted, who performed the survey and, most important — pick a candidate whose policies and personality appear best suited for the job.  

The most important takeaway is this: do your own research and don’t go with the crowd, because sometimes we have no idea where the crowd is actually headed.  

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

data.title: 8 killed in plane crash at remote Alaska radar site: US military
data.description:
Eight people were killed after the charter airplane they were traveling on crashed in Alaska on Thursday afternoon, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). 

The crash occurred near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, a U.S. Air Force military airstrip located in a remote area in the southwest part of the state.

U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis called the fatal crash a “devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve” in a statement reported by The Associated Press.

The crash occurred around 12:15 p.m. local time on Thursday, after the aircraft departed Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport en route to Cape Newenham, according to a preliminary FAA report. 

The agency said it will work jointly with the National Transportation Safety Board on an investigation into this crash. 

Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R) and Dan Sullivan (R) extended their thoughts and prayers following the news of this crash. 

“I join Alaskans in condolences as we learn of the plane crash in Cape Newenham today,” Murkowski wrote on social platform X.

“I’ve traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots,” the senator continued. “I appreciate the U.S. Coast Guard, NTSB, Alaska State Troopers, and the Rescue Coordination Center for responding to the site.”

She added, “Alaska is praying for those on board, their loved ones, and the team at Security Aviation.” 

Sullivan similarly expressed his condolences to the people who lost loved ones in this crash and said he will seek updates from the joint investigation. 

“Julie and I join our fellow Alaskans in praying for the families and loved ones of those who were killed today in a plane crash in Western Alaska,” he wrote online. “I’ve asked for a briefing from the NTSB and the FAA as we all seek answers on what caused this horrific tragedy.”

data.title: All red states should immediately audit their biggest school districts
data.description:
At the end of June, an audit of Jefferson County Public Schools was released to the public. The largest district in Kentucky, Jefferson County (which includes Louisville) enrolls almost 100,000 students — one in seven students in the state.

The report by auditor Allison Ball reveals the system’s complete institutional failure.

In 2024, Kentucky House Bill 6 compelled a special examination of Jefferson County schools and provided the funds to do so. Over the course of a few months, the auditing team reviewed over 2,000 documents from the 2022 through 2025 school years, visited schools, surveyed websites, and facilitated thousands of focus groups, interviews, and surveys.

The investigation reveals financial mismanagement, administrative bloat, and a school district without a clear direction, purpose or plan.

Reading the nearly 500-page report, what strikes one first is the flood of cash in which the district is drowning. Over 20 years, the per-pupil revenue has risen 62 percent, adjusted for inflation. Over the last decade, the school board approved the maximum property tax increase every single year. The report veers into exasperated disbelief when Ball writes that, despite receiving a bonus $500 million in additional funds during COVID, the district “somehow began running a budget deficit.”

Meanwhile, only 32 percent of elementary students scored as proficient readers on standardized tests. Did the money go to teachers? Nope. The average teacher salary has only increased by 12 percent over two decades.

In Ball’s words, the district has “a spending, not a revenue, problem.”

The list of concerns in the report is long. The district lacks a current and cohesive plan. Its board operates with too little focus on student outcomes. Twenty-six percent of its schools are under-enrolled. One fifth of all its students feel unsafe at school.

Stakeholders reported concerns about limited transparency and lack of input on the board’s decisions. Some teachers appeared uncertain or lacked clarity regarding curriculum content. The district has $1.3 billion in unmet facilities needs. For the 2022-23 and 2024-25 school years, 33,358 behavior incidents on buses were committed by repeat offenders — 78 percent of all such incidents.

Some of the most damning points in the report are the most prosaic. For example, no policy requires a written bid before the district enters into contracts with vendors.

By the end of the report, the reader is left with the impression that this district is filled with individuals with no clue how to manage the state’s largest school system.

This is not just a matter of woke Marxists trying to indoctrinate your children. Rather, it is an assemblage of mediocre to incompetent staff with no concept of governance, tradeoffs or management involved in running an organization. If this were a business, every single administrator in the school district would probably be fired, and the district would perform better as a result.

A district-wide breakdown such as this does not occur in a vacuum. Nor is this problem isolated to one school system in one state. Rather, a number of incentives and first principles make such systemic failure a norm in public K-12 education.

A refusal to acknowledge tradeoffs and limitations (a school cannot be all things to all students) means that districts chase too many goals and extend their resources far beyond their reasonable capacities. Traditional pipelines for leadership — from teacher to principal to district administrator — reward instructional excellence. But institutional leadership requires a different skillset from that of an excellent educator.

Despite financial mismanagement, an ever-increasing budget only rewards fiscal irresponsibility. Top-heavy personnel trees mean vampiric district offices suck away resources from schools before funds reach the classroom, teachers, and students.

And that is only the beginning.

These systemic issues are far too numerous for any one policy to fix. There is no one standardized test, curriculum, school choice policy, or funding formula that will shift all incentives, change all minds, and suddenly develop the operational excellence necessary to run a complex school system.

What are the answers? Well, there is fiscal austerity, strengthened personnel pipelines, better curriculum, increased accountability, slashed regulations and smarter pay structures, to name just a few. And notably, although I love highfalutin calls for a return to classical education and debates over first principles, this audit suggests a need for something much simpler first: a development of competence.

Can schools even keep the trains running on time, professional roles clarified and teachers knowledgeable of their curriculum?

A sober, comprehensive audit such as this one should be conducted everywhere. It provides an unsparing look into school districts’ straits, thereby emphasizing the need for comprehensive reform beyond mere funding increases. In fact, a thorough analysis of the report suggests that another blank check will only make matters worse — the same way another hit of a drug relieves symptoms in the moment but worsens addiction.

This audit lists not only complaints, but also recommendations for improvement.

Were every red state in the country to compel such audits of their largest school systems, the vastness of public education’s failures would become apparent. Pat answers would no longer suffice. Systemic failure requires comprehensive reform. The findings of this audit would be difficult for any district to face, but kudos to Kentucky for being willing at least to acknowledge them.

Other states would be wise to do the same.

Daniel Buck is a research fellow and the director of the Conservative Education Reform Network at the American Enterprise Institute.

data.title: Leaders can learn from Mike DeWine's gravity-defying political career
data.description:
Here is an underreported story about a high-ranking official who has defied political gravity. Over the last 49 years, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), age 79, has been elected and reelected to seven prestigious county, state and federal offices. Despite two setbacks, he kept moving on and up.

DeWine won his first election as Greene County Prosecutor (1977 to 1981). He then served in the Ohio state Senate (1981 to 1982), the U.S. House of Representatives (1983 to 1991), as Ohio lieutenant governor (1991 to 1995), and in the U.S. Senate (1995 to 2007), where he lost his first bid in 1992 and was later defeated in 2006, while seeking his third term. Undeterred, DeWine was elected Ohio attorney general (serving from 2011 to 2019) and then governor (from January 2019 to until this coming January, term-limited).

Outside Ohio, DeWine is barely known, but his electoral record is unlikely to be matched by any politician. He shared his lessons, telling me, “My biggest regrets are when I didn’t have all the facts or didn’t drill down deep enough before making an informed decision.” The governor cautioned, “It is important to acknowledge that you aren’t always the expert, find the experts who can give you the data you need, and listen to those you want to lead and encourage them to come up with ideas.”

It remains unclear whether DeWine will be succeeded this November by Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, whom he has endorsed, or by Democratic physician Amy Acton. Even in Ohio, where President Trump won by 11 points in 2024, the political forecast is cloudy, with a chance of Republican defeat.

Moreover, the prospect of Republicans losing control of the Senate looms over a special election between Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). DeWine has had his dealings with Brown, who walloped him in 2006 amid a tough year for Republicans nationwide and especially tough in Ohio.

This is a tangled saga. Then-Sen. Brown, running for his third term in 2024, was defeated by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Today, Brown is fighting to win the Senate seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance, which Gov. DeWine filled in January 2025 by appointing then-Lt. Gov. Husted.

DeWine is known for his resilience. After 12 years in the Senate, he returned to Ohio and taught government at several colleges before seeking elective office again. In 2010, he narrowly won the attorney general’s seat — an atypical post-Senate career move. He served under Gov. John Kasich (R).

After regaining his political momentum, Attorney General DeWine was overwhelmingly reelected in 2014. His work to test and develop criminal profiles from the massive backlog of rape-kits held by the state’s local law enforcement agencies — which laid bare the existence of 300 serial rapists in the state, who were linked to more than 1,100 crimes — helped propel him to his 2018 gubernatorial victory. Impressively, DeWine was reelected in 2022 by a 25-point margin.

Given DeWine’s remarkable journey through Washington and Ohio politics, he understands the fundamentals of leadership and governance. “Your mission and goals should always be clear and based on your core principles,” he explained. “Then, paint a picture of that vision so that people understand the ‘why’ behind it — why it’s important, why it matters, and why it will make a difference.”

DeWine emphasized, “You should be transparent and communicate what you know -and don’t know — focus on just a few big things, and then, be willing to make the tough decisions.”

That philosophy of focusing on “a few big things” is reflected in a recent stunning achievement; CNBC named Ohio “America’s top state for business 2026.” In his news release, DeWine stated, “When I took office, I promised to ‘plant the seeds’ of long-term investments that will positively impact Ohio for years to come. Today’s announcement is proof that these seeds are growing, and Ohio has a bright future ahead.”

After nearly five decades of continuous service, current and aspiring leaders can learn from Mike DeWine, a bespectacled, diminutive man who shuns the limelight. He is a workhorse who speaks truth to power, not a showhorse — the current political model.

When I asked Ann O’Donnell, the governor’s longtime chief advisor, how he managed to keep getting elected, she replied, “Mike DeWine is a radical optimist who believes deeply in the potential of all Ohioans. He loves Ohio and genuinely cares about the well-being of the people he has represented or governed.”

“Public service is both an incredible opportunity and an awesome responsibility,” DeWine told me. His advice to young officeholders: “Don’t waste time; treat every day you are in office with urgency while focusing on the things where you can make a difference.”

The governor also revealed his successful leadership style: “I taught my team a long time ago what we call the ‘but for’ test. But for you taking this action or that action, this change or the result would not have happened. If others are already doing it, then focus on something else.”

Regarding his remaining months in office, DeWine said, “I don’t spend much time thinking about legacy. Instead, I intend to help all Ohioans reach their full God-given potential.”

Summarizing her boss, chief advisor O’Donnell said, “He is the real deal, one of the last of a rare breed of public servants.”

Showhorse politicians, take note.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill.

data.title: Gen Z turns against capitalism as DSA takes off
data.description:
Only 9 percent of Americans under 30 have a “very positive” view of capitalism, according to a new CBS/YouGov poll. 

That shows a stark generation between Generation Z and older generations.

Thirty-three percent of people over 65, the Baby Boom generation, say they have a very positive view of capitalism, while 23 percent of people aged 45-64, a grouping that includes Gen Xers and older millennials, view capitalism very positively.

Millennials in the 30-44 age range were closer to Gen Z, with just 15 percent saying they had a very positive view of capitalism.

Forty-one percent of respondents under 30 had a very negative or somewhat negative view of capitalism. That compares to 27 percent of those 65 and older; 32 percent of those aged 45-64, and 37 percent of those aged 30-44.

The data arrives amid a surge in democratic socialist victories across the U.S. — and not just in progressive corners of the country. State Rep. Angie Nixon (D-Fla.) on Tuesday beat out the more moderate Alex Vindman (D) in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida, a state known for its sunshine, not socialism. 

Ashik Siddique, national co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), said the polling illustrates what the group is seeing at the street level: Generation Z is ready for a big change.

“We’ve seen that polling and it’s definitely striking, but to us, it really tracks with the experience that so many younger people have,” Siddique told The Hill. 

“Gen Z, especially by now, just like wasn’t even raised with a lot of the assumptions that I think millennials were,” he added. “Seeing the condition of the world today, our government spending so much money on militarism and expanding ICE and giving tax cuts to the billionaires to the tune of trillions of dollars while public services are being cut for most Americans – it’s just like the contrast is really clear.”

When asked if there’s a gap between disliking capitalism and desiring a socialist economic system, Siddique said that in response to the capitalist status quo, “people are way more open to socialism.”

He cited a 2025 poll from Jacobin and the DSA Fund which found that “Democrats prefer democratic socialism to capitalism by a 58-point margin.”

Nixon is seen as the underdog in the general election battle this fall.

In response to her primary win, election handicapper Sabato Crystal Ball shifted its projection for the seat from “likely Republican” to a safe Republican seat.

That’s partly because of the fundraising shortage Nixon is expected to have, but also reflects doubts that democratic socialism will be a winning message in the fall in Florida.

CBS/YouGov interviewed 2,287 U.S. adults between August 12-14 for their poll, which had a 2.6-point margin of error. 

— Abigail Walker

Split up: Gen Z is the generation most divided by gender

Gen Z is the generation most politically split by gender, and the difference could affect the midterms this November.

Former Vice President Harris won 63 percent of women and 46 percent of men aged 18-29 in 2024, per a Catalist analysis. The 17-point gap was the largest of all generations, and also the largest Catalist has measured across four election cycles.

Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) looked at ideological malleability in July and found that two-thirds of young adults have shifted their political views in recent years.

CIRCLE reported that 40 percent of young women’s beliefs remained unchanged, compared to 26 percent of young men’s. Among the women studied, 31 percent shifted to the left, 9 percent to the right, 11 percent to the center and 9 percent reported “other.” 

Among the men, 22 percent shifted to the left, 21 percent to the right, 16 percent to the center and 14 percent reported “other.”

Party is a really big driver of whether someone shows up to the ballot box,” Sara Suzuki, a senior researcher at CIRCLE, told The Hill. And across both genders — and probably most Americans — cost of living is a top concern. These factors could push people to the polls in November. 

A June Economist/YouGov poll pinned President Trump’s approval rating among adults 18-29 at minus 45, the lowest it’s been in his presidency.

This dissatisfaction, alongside historical trends that show midterm elections results serve as a reaction to who is in the White House, could mean that November may favor Democrats among Gen Z voters, according to Melissa Deckman, CEO of the Public Religion Research Institute. 

Deckman added that young women are the most progressive age group and tend to lean left compared to their male counterparts. But this drastic difference between the two genders is unique to Gen Z, and it may be due to today’s media landscape.

“Gen Z has grown up in a fragmented media culture, and algorithms send young women and young men to different sites,” Deckman told The Hill.

This was evident in 2024 when Harris appeared on Alex Cooper’s “Call Her Daddy,” a podcast with a mostly female audience, and Trump spoke with Joe Rogan, Theo Von and NELK with mostly male audiences. 

November will hold several close races, but if any candidate can yank across the Gen Z gender divide and pull across the aisle, they may have a better chance. “Young people go to the spheres they already belong to,” Suzuki said.

The CIRCLE study had a margin of error of 2.5 points and surveyed 5,549 adults between the ages of 18-29

 — Claire Leibowitz

Cashing out: Is Gen Z opting for sports betting as a form of investing?

Some Gen Zers appear to be using sports betting platforms as an investment strategy.

The legalization and growing accessibility of sports betting has made it easier than ever to download sportsbooks like DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM, alongside prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket.

Sports betting has expanded from a $400 million industry in 2018 into a nearly $17 billion industry in 2026, and a large slice of that is Gen Z.

According to a survey from personal finance platform Betterment, 52 percent of Gen Z sports bettors are putting money intended for investing into sportsbooks, a 21-percentage point lead over Millennials and 42-percentage point lead over Gen X.

Betterment’s survey was conducted between March 27 and April 3, 2026, interviewing a total of 1,000 U.S. respondents evenly split between Gen Z, millennials, Gen X and boomers.

About one in eight investors say sports betting is a part of their long-term investment strategy, which includes 26 percent of Gen Z. Thirty-six percent of Gen Z doesn’t participate in sports betting at all.

The reason why a large chunk of Gen Z is locked in on betting as an investment strategy is that young adults want a way to accelerate money made for long-term investing, or a “shortcut” as CNBC calls it. 

The National Council for Problem Gambling (NCPG) has identified trends in advertising, accessibility and Gen Z’s “hustle culture” that keep the generation hooked on making bets.

“When it comes to sports betting, the key items we’re identifying is responsiveness to advertising participation by mobile devices,” said Julia Brunson, communications manager for the NCPG. 

“Sports betting is gambling, it’s not investing, and our position is that sports betting should only be done as entertainment, not as a strategy for making money or building wealth,” Brunson continued. 

Brunson points out that Gen Z’s obsession over sports betting will most likely have an impact on Gen Alpha as well.

“[Gen Alpha] is currently interacting with sports betting products and prediction markets, they’re watching their older siblings do these things, they’re watching the games with them, you know, they’re engaging passively with advertising,” Brunson told The Hill.

Leaders in the sportsbook industry have also emphasized that placing money on sporting events is supposed to be fun, not an investment strategy.

“This is not confined to Gen Z or any other generation, sports betting is a form of entertainment.” a leader in the online gaming industry told The Hill. “It’s not a wealth creation vehicle so the adults that decide to engage with wagering or gaming, or, you know, casino play, are doing this within a predetermined entertainment budget, and should not be doing it with money that is either needed for savings or for any other essential expense.” 

In last week’s edition of The Feed, we reported on Gen Z’s growing reliance and trust in crypto.

There’s a parallel between crypto and sports betting. In both cases, Gen Z is looking to easily accessible platforms to make some quick money or develop hobbies.

“All types of industries are trying to meet the small net with these generations that are basically born as digital natives, and so accessibility is an important component of that,” the online gaming industry leader said about the parallels sports betting has with other platforms.

— Joshua Feldstein

Need support for gambling? Call or text 1-800-MY-RESET.

One last thing: The emojis you use may show your age 💯

You may be speaking a different language than people outside of your generation. That is, your emoji use might be aging you. 

According to a study from The New York Times, different generations use different emojis for the same reaction. For example, 😭,🤣 and 😂 were three of the most used emojis in 2025, but 😭 skyrocketed, particularly with teenage girls. In comparison, it was the least used among Gen X.

Although there are 24 other available heart emojis, Gen Alpha has adopted 🫰, and the symbol’s use has grown 109 percent in a year. (Look closely — the heart is at the cross in the fingers). 

The New York Times acquired the data from Reddit’s Academic Torrents, which published combined data from Pushshift and Arctic Shift by subreddit. Data was taken from November 2024 to January 2025 and November 2025 to January 2026. 

Emoji use data was collected with Google’s Federated Analytics, capturing anonymous use of the GBoard (the default keyboard on stock Android devices like Google Pixel).

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

data.title: Trump seeks to boost Darline Graham in South Carolina homestretch
data.description:
President Trump is seeking to give Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) a final boost as her candidacy hits a road bump in the race to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). 

Trump will hit the campaign trail Friday for Darline Graham, whom he appointed to fill out her brother’s term, ahead of her runoff election in the GOP primary Tuesday against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.). 

The race will stand as a test for the strength of Trump’s endorsement as Graham, a political novice, enters the arena. 

Her inexperience was on full display on the debate stage Tuesday, when she flubbed a national security question, drawing attacks on her fitness to serve in the Senate.

Trump and Graham are slated to campaign in Myrtle Beach, which is home to former Senate candidate Rep. Russell Fry’s (R-S.C.) district. Fry lost his bid for Senate in the initial Republican primary election to replace Graham and did not advance, making his support base critical for Norman and Graham. 

“Myrtle Beach is the exact correct place for them to go. It is the heart of Russell Fry’s district and home to probably the largest population of persuadable voters that we expect will be voting,” said Mick Mulvaney, who served in Trump’s first administration and represented South Carolina’s 5th Congressional District in the House. 

“Trump will obviously carry a lot of weight. But how much remains to be seen. Polling indicates that maybe only 40 percent of voters put a lot of weight on his endorsement,” he continued. 

“That, combined with her astonishingly poor performance in the debate earlier this week, may make this race much closer than people realize,” he said. 

During her primary debate against Norman on Tuesday, Graham was asked how Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues. Graham admitted “national security is not” her thing but that she supports the military. 

The answer marked a stark contrast between her and her late brother, who was seen as a key foreign policy leader in the Senate. It was also met with immediate criticism from Norman and his allies.

“Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate,” former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump in 2024 and is supporting Norman, said in a post on X. 

Norman told Kellie Meyer of NewsNation that Graham’s debate response was “serious.” 

“What is more serious is who she is getting supported by is everything I’m against,” he added.

Graham sought to clean up the comment during a sit-down interview on Fox News’s “Hannity” Wednesday, casting herself at the opposite of a career politician. 

“I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham said. 

Maggie Knox, a South Carolina GOP official who is not endorsing in the primary, characterized Graham’s answer as “an honest response.” 

“Could she have answered that better? Absolutely,” Knox told The Hill. “I had breakfast with someone this morning and she said, ‘I liked it that she didn’t pretend like she knew something she didn’t. That was kind of refreshing.’” 

Graham walks into Tuesday with an advantage from Trump’s endorsement and her status as Lindsey Graham’s sister. Trump won the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, by 11 points in 2020, and by 14 points in 2016. 

“Without Trump, Darline wouldn’t have a chance,” Mulvaney said. “And by that, I mean she’d be polling at very low, single digits.” 

A source with Graham’s campaign told The Hill that her team is relying on more than just the president’s backing to get across the finish line. 

“It opens a door, but it doesn’t walk you through it,” the source said, referring to Trump’s endorsement as “the gold standard” in politics. 

“People want to know that their candidate is going to work with President Trump, and that’s as, if not more, important than the endorsement,” the source said, citing Graham’s work since being appointed to the Senate by Trump. 

While Trump’s endorsement is objectively helpful, he does not have a perfect record in this cycle.

Earlier this week, Trump took losses when Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) lost his primary race, as well as his endorsed candidate for Florida’s 19th Congressional District.

Rep. Andy Ogles (R), who was backed by Trump, also lost his primary in Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District along with Rep. Randy Feenstra (R) in Iowa’s gubernatorial primary and Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (R) in Georgia’s gubernatorial primary. 

Trump issued a rare double endorsement of South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette (R) in June after Evette, his initial pick, failed to avoid a runoff election and later lost. 

While Norman has supported Trump’s second administration, he notably endorsed Haley over Trump for president in 2024. Additionally, as a member of the fiscally conservative House Freedom Caucus, Norman and his colleagues have not been afraid to push back on the administration and House Republican leadership. 

The source with Graham’s campaign argued that Norman would be “a caucus of one” and does not want to work with the president. 

Norman told NewsNation his support for Trump is “unwavering.” 

“Do I need a call? No. I’ll support him regardless because I believe in what he’s doing,” the congressman said. 

“The Senate has been the graveyard for every good thing [Trump] wants,” he said, adding that like Trump, he would like to “blow up” the filibuster. 

The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will go on to face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November.

“I think a lot of South Carolinians are looking at this and thinking who is more likely able to go against Annie Andrews and come out on top,” Knox said. 

Andrews faces an uphill climb in the red state. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as solid Republican. However, nationally Republicans are facing headwinds amid Trump’s declining approval ratings and rising Democratic enthusiasm. 

Trump’s approval rating in South Carolina sits at 42 percent, according to a Civiqs tracking poll.

“We know that this is a tough midterm. We know that we are up against a voting public that is certainly battling some voter fatigue, and we are trying to energize our party but it’s a tough row to hoe, I’m not going to lie,” Knox said.

“Are we super worried about Annie Andrews? No, but are we going to play it like we have it in the bag? Absolutely not,” she said. 

Kellie Meyer of NewsNation contributed.
